results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

* Keep any records that support an item of income or a deduction on a return **until the period of limitations for that return expires**. The IRS requires you to keep records for the length of time that could be needed to administer any provision of the Internal Revenue Code – that is, for the period of limitations that applies to the tax year for which the item was reported. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* For **employment‑tax records** (e.g., payroll, wage statements, Form 941/944 information), you must retain them for **at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* Keep **copies of your filed tax returns**; they help you prepare future returns and support amended filings. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* For **property or asset records** (e.g., depreciation, basis, sale of property), keep them **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* When records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do **not discard them until you confirm that no other government entity (e.g., insurer, creditor) requires a longer retention period**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

In short, most records stay on file for the period of limitations that applies to the return, with employment‑tax records required for at least 4 years.



**Sources:**

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several important reasons:

1. **Tax compliance and deduction support** –  
   *Your books must show your gross income, deductions, and credits, and the supporting documents that prove those numbers.  The IRS may test your records and can impose penalties if they are incomplete or inaccurate.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

2. **Building accurate financial statements** –  
   *Good records let you prepare income‑statement (profit‑and‑loss) and balance‑sheet reports, which help you track whether the business is improving, what items are selling, and what changes are needed.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

3. **Preparing tax returns** –  
   *The records you keep are the basis for all income, expense, and credit entries on your tax return.  The IRS can request to see these records any time it reviews a return; having them ready speeds the examination process.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

4. **Documentation for IRS inspections** –  
   *You must keep the records available at all times for inspection.  If the IRS examines your tax returns, they may ask you to explain the items reported; a complete set of records makes that easier.*  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

5. **Duration of retention matters** –  
   *You must keep records for the period of limitations of each return (e.g., up to 3 years for most returns, longer for employment‑tax records, asset depreciation, etc.).  Keeping them longer than required for the IRS may be useful if insurers or creditors need them.*  
   [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

6. **Business integrity and accountability** –  
   *Separate books for each business, daily entry of transactions, and a reconciled business checking account help you avoid errors and provide an accurate picture of how the business operates.*  
   [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

7. **Legal and regulatory reasons** –  
   *Certain types of records (e.g., minute‑books for a corporation, employment‑tax records, depreciation records for assets) are required by law for proper administration of tax and other regulatory duties.*  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12), [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

In short, keeping detailed, organized business records protects you from IRS penalties, ensures you can claim the deductions you are entitled to, and gives you the information you need to run and grow the business.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
**Short answer**

- **Use the cash method** if (a) you don’t keep inventory **or** (b) you keep inventory but qualify as a *small‑business taxpayer* and can treat the inventory as “non‑incidental” material or supplies.  
- **Use the accrual method** if you keep inventory and are **not** a small‑business taxpayer (or you want to match income and expenses more closely).  
- You may use a **combination method** only if the “accumulated‑income” side is segregated from the inventory side and inventory is handled on an accrual basis (unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer).  

You choose a method when you file your **first** income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C. After that, you must use the same method consistently, and any change requires IRS approval (Form 3115) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).

---

### 1.  What the IRS wants

| Requirement | What the IRS says | Where it appears |
|-------------|------------------|-----------------|
| **Method must show income clearly** | “You must use an accounting method that clearly shows your income.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Consistency** | “You must use the same accounting method to figure your taxable income and to keep your books.” | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Inventory rule** | If inventory is necessary, you must in most cases use an **accrual** method for the inventory portion, unless you are a small‑business taxpayer. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Small‑business exception** | Small‑business taxpayers (average annual receipts ≤ $31 million and not a tax shelter) may treat inventory as “non‑incidental” material or supplies and still use the cash method. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Combination method limits** | *If an inventory is necessary, you must generally use an accrual method for purchases and sales.*  The rest of the business can use cash, but the combination is treated as cash. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Changing methods** | “If you want to change your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval.”  File Form 3115. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17) |

---

### 2.  When to pick each method

| Situation | Recommended Method | Why |
|-----------|-------------------|-----|
| **No inventory, small receipts** | **Cash** | Simple; income when received, expenses when paid. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **No inventory, large receipts** | **Cash** | Still the simplest; inventory rules don’t apply. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **Has inventory, not a small‑business taxpayer** | **Accrual** | Inventory must be valued and tracked; accrual matches revenues and costs in the same year. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Has inventory, small‑business taxpayer** | **Cash** *or* **Accrual for inventory only** | Small‑business rule allows cash, or you may treat inventory as non‑incidental material and keep cash. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards you should carry out a **routine workplace self‑inspection** and follow a systematic approach that combines a safety program, a structured checklist, and external resources.  

---

### 1.  Start with a formal safety and health program  
- **Why:** A program gives you a framework for finding and fixing hazards before they cause injury.  
- **What to do:**  
  * Make sure you have a written safety and health program that is reviewed regularly.  
  * Include worker participation, management leadership, hazard identification, hazard prevention, training, program evaluation, and communication.  
- **Segment:** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9) – outlines the core elements and the need for a written program.  

### 2.  Conduct a routine self‑inspection  
- **How:**  
  * Have knowledgeable and experienced workers (or a team that includes them) walk through the entire workplace each time.  
  * Use a **self‑inspection checklist** that matches the general‑industry categories covered in the handbook.  
  * If your industry is construction, maritime, or agriculture, use the appropriate industry checklist (the handbook notes that the general checklists do not cover these sectors).  
- **What to record:**  
  * Identify hazards.  
  * Note whether controls are in place and whether they are effective.  
  * Record any new hazards that appear.  
- **Segment:** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) – describes the purpose of self‑inspections, the use of checklists, and the need to monitor and evaluate controls.  

### 3.  Compile and analyze supporting data  
- **What to include:**  
  * Accident and injury records (e.g., OSHA 300 log).  
  * Worker training logs.  
  * Maintenance and incident reports.  
- **Purpose:** Helps determine where hazards are most acute and whether existing controls work.  
- **Segment:** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) – "Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records…"

### 4.  Review applicable OSHA standards  
- **Why:** Some hazards may already be governed by a specific OSHA standard.  
- **What to do:**  
  * Identify which subpart of 29 CFR (e.g., Subpart H for hazardous materials) applies to your business.  
  * Read the standard’s introduction and analyze hazards in context of your workplace, equipment, materials, and workers.  
- **Segment:** [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91) – explains how to find which standards apply and how to interpret them.  

### 5.  Use additional resources to fill gaps  
- **On‑Site Consultation:**  
  * Request a free, confidential consultation visit from your local OSHA On‑Site Consultation program.  
  * Consultants can help perform a thorough hazard assessment and recommend controls.  
- **Additional references:**  
  * OSHA’s safety and health program self‑evaluation tool.  
  * OSHA’s implementation checklist and audit tool.  
- **Segment:** [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90) – details the On‑Site Consultation Program and its benefits.  

### 6.  Document and act on findings  
- **Document:**  
  * Keep a written record of each inspection, the hazards found, controls implemented, and follow‑up actions.  
- **Act:**  
  * Immediately control identified hazards.  
  * If a control cannot be implemented right away, document a plan and timeline.  
  * Review and update the safety program annually or sooner if conditions change.  
- **Segments:** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) – all discuss documentation, control, and program review.  

### 7.  Repeat regularly  
- **Frequency:** Conduct self‑inspections at a routine interval (e.g., monthly, quarterly) that fits your business size and hazard profile.  
- **Why:** Regular inspections help catch new hazards early and keep controls effective.  
- **Segment:** [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) – “routine workplace self‑inspections” is repeatedly emphasized.  

---

#### Quick checklist to use during each inspection  

| Step | Action | Reference |
|------|--------|-----------|
| 1 | Walk the entire facility | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| 2 | Use the provided self‑inspection checklist | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| 3 | Record hazards and current controls | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| 4 | Compare findings with OSHA standards | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91) |
| 5 | Compile data with injury/illness and training logs | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |
| 6 | Draft corrective action plan | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| 7 | Update safety program documentation | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9) |
| 8 | Schedule next inspection | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8) |

By following this structured approach you ensure that hazards are identified, evaluated, controlled, and re‑evaluated in a systematic way, keeping your workplace safe and compliant.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. Accrual accounting – the key difference**

| Feature | **Cash method** | **Accrual method** |
|---------|------------------|--------------------|
| **When income is counted** | When you actually receive (or constructively receive) the money. | When you earn the income – the date the sale or service is performed, even if you don't receive payment yet. |
| **When expenses are counted** | When you actually pay the money (or when the payment becomes payable). | When the expense is incurred – the date the goods were received or the service performed, even if you don't pay yet. |
| **Typical use** | Most sole‑proprietors and small businesses with no inventory. | Businesses that sell inventory or credit customers, or that want to match income and expenses in the same year. |

*Why it matters:* “The purpose of an accrual method of accounting is to match income and expenses in the correct year.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Examples**

- *Cash:* If you receive a check on Jan 4, 2025 but haven’t deposited it until Jan 5, 2025, you still include the money in 2025 income because you *constructively* received it that year.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

- *Accrual:* You sell a computer on Dec 28, 2025, bill the client in early January 2026, and receive payment in Feb 2026.  Under accrual, you include that income in 2025 because *all events that fix your right to receive the income have occurred* that year.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

- *Cash expenses:* If you pay an insurance premium in 2025 for coverage that starts July 1, 2025, you deduct the amount in the year the payment is made – 2025 – even though the coverage began later.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

- *Accrual expenses:* If you buy office supplies in December 2025, receive the bill in December and pay it in January 2026, you can deduct the expense in 2025 because the liability and economic performance occurred in that year.  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**Summary**

- **Cash method** is simple: record money when it moves in or out of your account.  
- **Accrual method** tracks money *earned* and *incurred* regardless of when the cash changes hands, giving a picture of economic performance that matches income with the expenses that helped produce it.

When you choose a method, you have to use it consistently for both calculating taxable income and keeping your books, and you can’t switch without IRS approval unless you meet specific automatic‑change rules.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
**Yes – you can deduct ordinary and necessary business‑travel expenses, but only the portions that are strictly for your trade or business.**  

- **Transportation:** Airfare, train, bus, car rentals, taxis, limousines, faxes, and other business‑related travel can be deducted.  If you use your own vehicle, you may deduct either  actual running costs *or* the 2025 standard mileage rate of **70 ¢ per business mile** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35).  If you rent a car, you may deduct only the portion that is business use [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  

- **Meals and lodging:** You can deduct lodging costs for an overnight or otherwise extended stay that is necessary for your duties.  For meals you may use actual expenses or the prescribed standard allowance, but only **50 % of the cost is deductible** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  

- **Other travel‑related costs:** Baggage, shipping, parking, tolls, telephone calls, tips, and dry‑cleaning while on a business trip are deductible as business expenses [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41); you can also deduct business‑use portions of car‑related expenses such as gas, oil, tires, repairs, insurance (if you use the standard mileage rate you cannot deduct the insurance premium) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  

- **Commuting:** Transportation expenses between your home and your regular place of business (your “tax home”) are **not deductible** as business travel [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35).  

- **Record‑keeping:** Keep receipts or other documentation proving the expense was ordinary, necessary, and related solely to business purpose.  Reference Pub. 463 for detailed guidance [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  

- **Limits & qualifications:** The expenses must be ordinary (common in your trade) and necessary (helpful and appropriate).  Any portion that is also personal in nature must be excluded from the deduction [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32).  

In short, if you travel away from home for business, you can deduct transportation, lodging, 50 % of meals, and other related costs, allocating business versus personal portions as required.  Follow the rules above and retain proper records to support your deduction.

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is a short, one‑ or two‑paragraph snapshot that gives the reader a quick overview of what you plan to accomplish with your business. It should include:

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, follow the steps that the guidance in the plan outlines:

1. **Identify the niche** – state who your best customer is.  
   *“Describe your market niche; who is your best customer.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **Segment the customer base** – choose the criteria that make sense for your business.  
   *Business markets are classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.*  
   *Consumer markets are segmented by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Define their characteristics** – give concrete traits for the group you’ve identified.  
   *“Identify those customers and describe their characteristics.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate size and growth potential** – use data such as population figures, sales tax information, and industry reports to quantify the market.  
   *“Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc.”*  
   *“Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Integrate the description in the marketing section** – place the target‑market narrative in the Marketing part of the business plan, where it supports your product, pricing, and promotion strategies.  
   *“The marketing plan includes information on the total market with an emphasis on your target market.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

> Our target market is small‑to‑mid‑size restaurants in the 34‑mile radius of downtown Springfield that serve farm‑to‑table cuisine. The local farm‑to‑table segment has grown 8 % annually over the past three years, giving us an estimated target pool of 150 businesses and a market share goal of 5 % within five years.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  
If you own or operate a shop that serves the public, the U.S. ADA requires that you make the facility “accessible” to people with disabilities, unless it is **impossible or not reasonably achievable** to do so.  The law applies to all private businesses of all sizes, regardless of how long the business has existed or how many employees you have.  

- The ADA’s Title III defines a “public accommodation” as a private business that provides goods or services to the public, and it imposes accessibility requirements on such facilities. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
- Even if your shop was built before the 1992‑1993 “new‑facility” dates, you still must remove any barriers that are “readily achievable” and provide accessibility where it can be done without undue expense or risk. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=5)

Typical requirements that you will need to address (if they are readily achievable) include:  

| What | Minimum/Typical requirement (from the ADA Standards) | Source |
|------|--------------------------------------------------------|--------|
| **Accessible entrance** | At least one entry that has no steps, ramps with slope not steeper than 1:12, handrails, and a 36‑inch wide clear width. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Accessible parking** | For every 25–50 allowable spaces, at least one space that includes a 5‑foot‑wide access aisle, an international symbol of accessibility, and a 98‑inch vertical clearance. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Sales or service counters** | A counter or auxiliary counter that is no higher than 36 inches above the floor and provides a 30” × 48” clear floor space in front of it. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Door hardware** | Door handles that are lever‑type or other “grab‑free” designs, and doors that are at least 36 inches wide. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Aisles and circulation** | A minimum of 36‑inch wide accessible routes that allow turning space (e.g., 60‑inch diameter for a 180° turn). | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |

If you cannot implement all of these measures, the ADA allows you to offer **alternative services** (e.g., curb‑side delivery or home service) while work on accessibility is completed.  That too is still a requirement to provide some non‑discriminatory means for the customer to access goods or services. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  

**Bottom line:**  
Yes, you are required to make your shop wheelchair accessible (or provide an equally effective alternative) if it is reasonably achievable under the ADA.  If there are barriers you cannot overcome right now, document the barriers and your plan to eliminate them as soon as resources allow.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are exempt from OSHA’s injury and illness record‑keeping rules only if **both** of the following conditions are true for the calendar year that just ended:

| Condition | What it means | How to confirm it |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------|
| 1️⃣ **Ten or fewer employees** | Your business had 10 or fewer workers for *every* day of the last calendar year. | Count the employees you had on each day of the year (or keep a simple “employees per day” record). |
| 2️⃣ **Low‑hazard industry** | Your business is listed in *29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A* as a low‑hazard industry. | Check that appendix: it lists industries such as grocery stores, restaurants, and chapels that are exempt. |

If **either** of those conditions is not met, you are *not* exempt and must keep OSHA injury and illness records. The records you must keep include:

* **OSHA Form 300** (log of work‑related injuries and illnesses) for any recordable injury or illness that is **not** a minor first‑aid case.  
* **OSHA Form 301** (incident report) for each recordable injury or illness.  
* **OSHA Form 300A** (annual summary) at the end of each calendar year.  

Even if you are exempt from full record‑keeping, you **still must** report certain serious incidents to OSHA:

* All work‑related **fatalities**.  
* All in‑patient **hospitalizations**.  
* All **amputations** and **loss of an eye**.  
These reports must be made to OSHA within **8 hours** of a fatality and within **24 hours** for hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye.

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax‑related records** – These records are needed to support everything you report on your federal tax return and to satisfy the IRS if it reviews your books.  
- **Income and expense documentation** – sales slips, invoices, receipts, bank deposit slips, cancelled checks, payroll records, and any other documents that show the amounts and sources of your gross receipts and the expenses you deduct. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
- **Copies of filed tax returns** – keep each return you file and any amended returns because they help you prepare future returns and prove what you claimed. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Employment‑tax records** – if you have employees, keep all records that support the amounts of employment taxes (Social‑Security, Medicare, federal income‑tax withholding, FUTA, etc.) for at least **four years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Asset‑related records** – if you own property used in your business (machinery, equipment, real‑estate, etc.) keep documents that show when and how you acquired the asset, its purchase price, cost of improvements, depreciation taken, Section 179 deductions, disposal details, and sale price. Keep these until the period of limitations expires for the year you dispose of the property. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Other support documents** – invoices, canceled checks, payroll journals, petty‑cash slips, and any other paper or electronic logs that back up the entries in your accounting books. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
- **Retention period for most tax records** – hold them at least until the period of limitations for the return runs out. The exact limitation period varies: usually 3 years for a regular income‑tax return, 6 years for nondeductible expenses or “enough‑to‑defend” situations, and some are “not limited” when fraud or false returns are involved. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Special cases** – if you dispose of an asset, keep the related records until the limitations period for that year of disposition ends. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

---

**Injury‑and‑illness records (OSHA)** – OSHA requires employers to keep a log of work‑related injuries and illnesses and related documentation.  
- **OSHA Forms**  
  - **Form 300** (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)  
  - **Form 301** (Injury and Illness Incident Report) – a supplementary report for each recordable case.  
  - **Form 300‑A** (Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) – an annual summary.  
  All these forms must be kept on the worksite (or in an electronic system that satisfies OSHA’s requirements). [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- **Medical and exposure records** – keep any records that document a worker’s medical treatment or exposure to hazardous substances for the time period required for that specific type of record. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- **Training records** – maintain records of required employee training and make them available for review. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- **Retainment period** – keep injury and illness records (Forms 300, 300‑A, 301) for a minimum of **five years**. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
- **Reporting requirements** – if you have 100+ workers in a high‑hazard industry, electronically submit the Form 300A summary to OSHA by March 2 of the following year; if you have 20–249 workers in certain high‑hazard industries, you must do the same as well. All fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye must be reported within the specified hours. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**1. Pick a legal form for your business**  
- The most common options are a sole proprietorship, partnership, S‑corporation, C‑corporation, or LLC. The choice determines the tax form you will file and the types of taxes you owe. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

**2. Get a taxpayer identification number (TIN)**  
- If you are a sole proprietor you can use your Social‑Security number, but you may obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you have employees or want a separate business number. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
- Applying for an EIN automatically enrolls the business in the Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS) for tax deposits. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)

**3. Decide on a tax year**  
- Either a calendar year (January 1 – December 31) or a fiscal year ending on the last day of a month other than December. Choose when you file your first return; changing later requires Form 1128. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**4. Choose an accounting method**  
- Cash method: income when received, expenses when paid.  
- Accrual method: income when earned, expenses when incurred. Use accrual if inventory is required; many small businesses use cash. Any change later requires IRS approval. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**5. Set up a bookkeeping system**  
- Use a single‑entry system (daily and monthly cash summaries) or a double‑entry system (journals and ledgers). The system must clearly show your income and expenses. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)  
- Keep a business checkbook, a summary of receipts, a disbursements journal, depreciation worksheets, and employee compensation records if applicable. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

**6. Keep supporting documents**  
- Store all receipts, invoices, bank statements, canceled checks, and electronic copies. Organize them by year and type (income, expense, asset). [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
- The IRS allows electronic record‑keeping as long as the system can produce legible, complete records and can be tested for compliance. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

**7. File the correct tax returns**  
| Business type | Primary form | Notes |
|--------------|--------------|-------|
| Sole proprietor | 1040 with Schedule C (and Schedule SE if self‑employment tax applies) | 1040‑ES is used for estimated tax. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)[[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| Partnership | 1065 | Pass‑through income to partners. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| S‑corp | 1120‑S | Use Schedule SE for owners. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |
| C‑corp | 1120 | Include payroll taxes if you pay employees. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6) |

**8. Pay estimated and employment taxes on time**  
- Estimated tax payments are due on the 15th of April, June, September, and the 15th of the month following your tax year’s end. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  
- If you have employees, file quarterly payroll tax returns (Form 941) and pay the payroll taxes through EFTPS. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)  
- File year‑end unemployment (FUTA) tax (Form 940) by January 31. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)

**9. File information returns**

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
**Keeping your employees safe** and **making your premises accessible** are two separate, but complementary, sets of requirements.  The documents you have provide specific actions you can take for each.

---

## 1.  Safety & Health of Employees  
| What to do | Source |
|------------|--------|
| **Implement a formal safety & health program** that includes management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification, prevention/control, training, evaluation, and communication.  Use OSHA’s recommended‑practice checklist to guide you. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Conduct regular workplace inspections** (internal or with workers) to find and fix hazards before they cause injury. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=10) |
| **Keep walking‑working surfaces clear, dry and slip‑resistant**; repair holes, spills, and obstructions promptly.  Provide guardrails where needed. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78) |
| **Maintain machinery and equipment safely**: keep them clean, provide clear labeling, emergency stop buttons, lock‑out provisions, splash guards, and adequate clearance. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=54) |
| **Keep OSHA record‑keeping up to date** (Forms 300/300A/301) and report required incidents (fatalities, hospitalizations, amputations, etc.) on time.  Keep records for the required periods. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Educate employees** on hazards, safe work practices, and the rights/recourses they have (e.g., whistleblower protection). | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91) |
| **Adopt a whistleblower‑friendly policy** that protects workers from retaliation for reporting safety concerns. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=93) |
| **Provide appropriate PPE and training for specific tasks** (e.g., chemical handling, electrical work). | (OSHA standards referenced in Segment 26, not explicitly listed here) |

## 2.  Accessibilty of the Premises  
| What to do | Source |
|------------|--------|
| **Make at least one entrance accessible**: either a ramp (max 1:12 slope, 36‑in. width, handrails), a lift, or an alternate door that is unlocked when the business is open.  If you use a turnstile, provide an accessible opening ≥32 in. wide. | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10), [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=13) |
| **Install signage** that clearly points from any inaccessible entrance to the accessible one.  Signposted gates or doors must be mounted at an accessible height (≤48 in. from the floor). | [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10), [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Provide accessible door hardware** (lever handles, loop handles, thumb‑latch‑free or disableable) so people who cannot grasp or twist can open the door. | [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Keep the approach to the building entry slip‑resistant, level, and free of steps**.  Add edge protection on ramps or landing areas to prevent rolling off. | [[12]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |
| **Offer accessible parking**: at least one space per 25–50 parking spaces (if ≤25 spaces, one; if ≤50, two).  Include an access aisle ≥5 ft. (cars) or ≥8 ft. (vans), a clear 98‑in. vertical height, signage with the international symbol, and a 120‑ft drive‑way with ≤1:50 slope. | [[13]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8), [[14]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) |

| **Make service counters accessible**: a lowered section at least 60 in. long and ≤34 in. high; or provide an auxiliary counter nearby. | [[17]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Adjust policies** so that disabled persons may bring service animals, request alternative communication methods, or use an accessible entrance that is kept unlocked during normal hours.  If a door stays locked, provide a publicly accessible buzzer or call box mounted on an accessible route. | [[18]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=18) |
| **Prioritize removal of architectural barriers** in the following order: 1) entrance access from street/parking; 2) internal access to sale or service areas; 3) public restrooms; 4) drinking fountains, telephones, etc.  Deviation from full compliance is permitted only if it poses no significant risk and the barrier removal is not “readily achievable.” | [[19]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) |
| **Document all accessibility changes** and keep a record of who performed the work, the date, and any cost savings or trade‑offs. | (Practical best practice; implied in ADA guidance) |

### Putting it together

3. **Schedule routine reviews** (e.g., quarterly) to verify that ramps, door hardware, parking, and interior routes remain in compliance.  
4. **Keep documented records** of inspections, repairs, training, and accessibility modifications—required for OSHA reporting and for an ADA complaint response.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
- If your business will **hire employees** or pay **Federal Excise Tax**, you are required to obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN).  
- If you don't have employees, you can still choose to get an EIN to use in place of your Social Security number, which can simplify record‑keeping and keep your personal SSN private. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  

**What accounting method do you choose?**  
- The IRS does not tie a particular accounting method to having an EIN.  
- When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business, you must **select an accounting method** that clearly shows your income. You can generally use:  
  - **Cash method** – records income when received and expenses when paid (common for sole proprietors with no inventory).  
  - **Accrual method** – records income when earned and expenses when incurred (mandatory if you keep inventory, unless you qualify as a small business).  
  - **Special or combination methods** for certain items or to meet specific circumstances. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

The accounting method you pick is independent of whether you have an EIN; you simply pick the method that best matches your business activities and inventory needs. If you have inventory, you will likely need the accrual method unless you qualify as a small business, but this decision is made **after** obtaining your EIN, if you need one.

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
You should keep the OSHA injury‑and‑illness record forms that your business is required to file:

* **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
* **OSHA Form 301** – the Injury and Illness Incident Report (a supplementary record for each recordable case)  
* **OSHA Form 300A** – the Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses that is filed annually  

These forms must be kept at the worksite for **at least five (5) years** after the date the injury or illness occurred.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14) lists the required OSHA forms; [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) specifies the five‑year retention requirement.

results.question: how do i register a trademark
results.answer:
To register a trademark, you can choose to file at the state level or at the federal level.  
- **State registration**: File through the Secretary of State’s office. In South Dakota, the office can be reached at (605) 773‑2797 or online at https://sdsos.gov/.  
- **Federal registration**: File with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). Contact the USPTO at (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, or visit www.uspto.gov.  

Before filing, search the trademark databases to ensure the name has not already been trademarked. Once you decide on the venue, submit the appropriate application and required fees to the chosen office.
